title: Justice for a Coptic boy
hook: a well-known report tells how Umar punished a governor's son for striking an Egyptian: since when have you enslaved people born free

segments.voice: Yesterday, Umar at al-Quds, stepping outside so a church would stay a church. Your line was: he prayed outside. Whose space did you leave as you found it? Day eight hundred seventy-four.

A horse race in Egypt. Two young men, two horses, and the wrong one wins. The winner is a Copt, an Egyptian Christian. The loser is the son of the governor, Amr ibn al-As, the man who rules the province for Umar. And the governor's son does what a certain kind of powerful young man does when he loses. He takes a whip to the winner, and as he strikes he says: take that, I am the son of the noble ones. Today: justice for a Coptic boy.
screen: `A HORSE RACE IN EGYPT.` → `THE GOVERNOR'S SON LOSES.` → `I AM THE SON OF THE NOBLE ONES.`

segments.voice: The story comes from a history of the conquest of Egypt, not from the hadith collections. It is a report people tell, not a verified hadith. The Copt doesn't take the beating quietly. He travels all the way to Medina and stands before Umar. Umar listens, and sends for the governor and his son to come too. When they arrive, Umar hands the whip to the Egyptian. Strike, he says, the son of the noble ones. And the Copt does. Then Umar turns to the governor himself, the father, the powerful man whose name had made his son feel untouchable, and says the line the story is remembered for: since when have you enslaved people, when their mothers bore them free? Listen to what that claims. Free from the womb. Not free because of your father's rank, or your tribe, or your faith. Free because you were born. And notice who stands where. A Christian subject of a Muslim state crosses a desert to accuse the son of a Muslim governor, and the caliph hands him the whip. The Qur'an calls for this kind of evenhandedness: it tells believers to stand firm for justice as witnesses for God, even against themselves, or their parents, or their kin, whether rich or poor. The story puts that verse on a dusty road between Egypt and Medina. Whatever happened on that road, the line is why the story lasts. Born free.
screen: `A REPORT, NOT A HADITH.` · `THE COPT CROSSES TO MEDINA.` · `UMAR HANDS HIM THE WHIP.` · `JUSTICE, EVEN AGAINST YOUR KIN.` · then, large: `WHEN THEIR MOTHERS BORE THEM FREE.`

segments.voice: The practice: defend someone's dignity. Sit up a little, breathe, and bring to mind a person who gets treated as smaller than they are. Someone who cleans your office. A new kid at school. A neighbor whose accent people mock. Breathe in, and say to yourself, about them: born free. Breathe out. Now think of one moment this week when you could stand up for them, even quietly. Using their name. Correcting a joke. Thanking them in front of others. Choose it. The bell holds the time.
Copt, an Egyptian Christian: the young man a governor's son struck with a whip, until Umar handed him the whip himself and asked, since when have you enslaved people born free? Today's word.
Your line: born free. Today, treat one person the world overlooks as exactly as free and as worthy as anyone. Day eight hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Muslims often quote Umar's line 'since when have you enslaved people when their mothers bore them free?' in sermons and writing on justice and human dignity, though the report comes from history, not the hadith collections.
